S0196.summary: Lee and colleagues use SHAP descriptions and Mahalanobis distance to identify suspicious changes in a domain-generation-algorithm detector. The method supplements distribution monitoring with information about how a classifier reaches its decisions. Its monitoring stage reduces dependence on immediate labels, while historical class information and labelled validation remain relevant to the experimental design.
S0196.interpretation: This is direct prior work for explanation-based drift monitoring. The project should compare against it rather than describe the use of SHAP for drift as a new idea. The study does not establish a CloudTrail retraining benefit or prove that explanation movement identifies an attack.

CORE05.summary: Maseno and colleagues test recurrent intrusion detectors under clean and adversarial network-flow conditions. LSTM and GRU models are stressed with FGSM and PGD, while SHAP displacement and feature-overlap information are used as secondary detection signals. Learned explanation-based detection is compared with a rule-based approach, and the paper distinguishes a small Kernel SHAP branch from larger GradientExplainer experiments.
CORE05.interpretation: Explanation drift is informative but not perfectly separable in this evaluation. Adversarial perturbation experiments must not be described as natural temporal CloudTrail drift. Overlapping sequence construction and partitioning warrant a leakage check; the available description raises a question, not proof of realised leakage.

CORE07.summary: Adediran and colleagues evaluate retrieval-augmented Gemini interpretation of CloudTrail events. Their knowledge sources include MITRE ATT&CK, AWS threat techniques and threat reports. The evaluation uses 200 annotated events sampled from a controlled Stratus Red Team environment, including malicious and benign examples. The reported comparison concerns contextual event interpretation and technique mapping rather than an adaptive statistical anomaly detector.
CORE07.interpretation: This is direct CloudTrail evidence, but its individual events do not establish a longitudinal drift benchmark. Reported performance numbers contain presentation differences that require reconciliation before numerical reuse. Simulator markers, annotation provenance and the absence of a publicly available temporal replication set are important review questions.

S0120.summary: This study applies a balanced, stacked Random Forest to DNS-over-HTTPS attack detection using CIRA-CIC-DoHBrw-2020. Explanation methods identify the traffic features influencing predictions, addressing the difficulty of inspecting encrypted DNS traffic. The authors report strong classification performance within their evaluated dataset.
S0120.interpretation: The work demonstrates an application-specific explanation pipeline. Its classification scores should not be transferred to cloud audit events, and high within-dataset performance does not itself establish resistance to future distribution changes.

S0206.summary: The proposed industrial-IoT detector combines an incremental stacking ensemble with active learning. A voting layer extends the stacking model, while committee-based querying and a modified nearest-neighbour component support learning from known and unfamiliar attacks. The central motivation is that an offline model becomes less useful as intrusion patterns change.
S0206.interpretation: This is relevant to label-efficient adaptation. Active querying nevertheless requires access to labels or an annotation process. It is not a label-free retraining baseline unless that additional supervision is made explicit.

E261.summary: The authors investigate a small set of network-flow features shared across several IoT intrusion datasets. They apply feature selection to TON-IoT, Aposemat IoT-23 and IoT-ID, then use SHAP to interpret the retained inputs. The resulting compact representation is evaluated for classification performance and prediction cost.
E261.interpretation: A common feature vocabulary may simplify comparisons between environments. Shared network-flow features are not the same as CloudTrail API, identity or service fields, so a cloud-audit implementation still needs domain-specific feature definitions.

S0043.summary: Kuppa and Le Khac address security drift by identifying shifted samples and discovering previously unseen classes. Their approach uses contrastive representations and nearest-class-mean reasoning, with experiments on security-relevant network and command-and-control data. Attacker-induced changes are considered alongside the usual challenge of evolving data distributions.
S0043.interpretation: The work motivates separating adaptation to genuinely new behaviour from unsafe learning of attacker-controlled records. Withheld-class and adversarial experiments provide controlled evidence; they do not substitute for chronological CloudTrail deployment or show that automatic retraining is always safe.

S0112.summary: This two-stage detector first trains an XGBoost intrusion classifier and computes SHAP explanations. An autoencoder then learns from those explanations to distinguish previously encountered attacks from unfamiliar ones. The reported evaluation uses NSL-KDD and compares detection of new test-time attacks with established intrusion-detection approaches.
S0112.interpretation: The paper shows that explanations can become model inputs rather than merely plots for analysts. Novel-attack discrimination is a different task from deciding when a production model should be updated, and the dataset does not represent cloud audit semantics.

S0090.summary: The authors combine ensemble deep learning with SHAP and LIME for industrial-IoT intrusion detection. ToN-IoT is used for evaluation, with an extreme-learning-machine detector among the comparisons. The explanation layer is intended to help analysts understand why traffic is blocked or classified as malicious.
S0090.interpretation: The study supports evaluating detection and explanation together. It does not follow that displaying feature importance reduces false alarms or provides a validated drift trigger; those benefits require their own measured outcomes.

S0091.summary: This paper develops dynamic feature selection for streaming intrusion detection. Its enhanced framework periodically invokes NSGA-II to balance classification error and memory use, with alternative rules for selecting a solution from the resulting candidates. Synthetic and real-data experiments compare the proposal with earlier feature-selection methods.
S0091.interpretation: Changing the selected feature set is an adaptation mechanism in its own right. A comparison with a SHAP-coupling policy should account for the feature-selection budget, update schedule and supervision assumptions rather than compare headline scores from different protocols.

S0092.summary: The Dynamic Feature Aware GP Ensemble extends a genetic-programming combiner with variable-length particle-swarm feature selection. It targets changing feature relevance in intrusion streams, rather than treating a single selected subset as permanently useful. The reported evaluation includes HIKARI 2021 and TON-IoT 2020 and considers predictive performance and memory use.
S0092.interpretation: Feature relevance can change even when the input schema stays fixed. This gives a useful comparator for attribution monitoring, but the paper's definition of feature drift must be distinguished from marginal input-distribution drift.

S0195.summary: The proposed system combines secure adaptive windowing with an authentication mechanism and a classifier for identifying malicious network activity. Its evaluation considers concept-drift behaviour together with detection quality and networking outcomes such as throughput and delay. The paper frames both attacker behaviour and changing benign behaviour as sources of model mismatch.
S0195.interpretation: This is supporting evidence for window-based adaptation. Networking performance, event classification and drift identification are separate endpoints and should not be combined into a single claim of security improvement.

S0277.summary: The EMNCD method combines non-parametric statistical tests to localise changes in IoT data streams. Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Wilcoxon rank-sum and Mann-Kendall tests are used within sliding-window analysis, alongside anomaly-detection and adaptation components. Artificial streams and an industrial-IoT intrusion dataset provide the reported evaluation settings.
S0277.interpretation: Localising a change point is useful for explaining when a detector's operating conditions shifted. The review should keep change-point quality separate from attack-detection quality and should report the journal's online and issue dates without assuming they are identical.

E283.summary: This study modifies a genetic-programming ensemble with online sequential extreme-learning-machine variants, balancing and classifier-update components. Several forms of concept drift are evaluated, together with intrusion benchmarks including KDD Cup 99, CICIDS-2017, CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 and ISCX 2012. Knowledge preservation and feature adaptation are important components of the proposal.
E283.interpretation: The authors also report a weakness on blip drift, which should remain visible in the synthesis. A method's success on several drift types is not evidence that it handles every transition or that its benchmark results transfer to AWS audit logs.

E403.summary: The study evaluates machine-learning intrusion detection for vehicular ad hoc networks and applies LIME to explain a Random Forest classifier. Its experiments report classification outcomes such as accuracy, recall and F1 on an application-layer traffic dataset. The explanation goal is to make individual intrusion decisions understandable.
E403.interpretation: This is a domain-specific example of local explanation. A perfect reported classification score must be interpreted within its dataset and partitioning protocol, not as proof of error-free operation in a new vehicle network or cloud environment.

E294.summary: The proposed IoMT intrusion detector uses fuzzy-based control to adjust LSTM training, including the number of epochs and early stopping. The authors compare it with other detection models and discuss problems caused by fixed training settings. The intended benefit is a better balance between underfitting and overfitting.
E294.interpretation: Adaptive training effort is not automatically the same as detecting concept drift. This paper is useful for distinguishing training-configuration adaptation from a measured response to an independently identified change in the data stream.

S0048.summary: This adaptive hybrid detector targets attacks on RPL in 6LoWPAN networks. Incremental classifiers and drift detectors, including ADWIN, DDM and EDDM, are evaluated under changing mobility and malicious-node conditions. The study extends beyond a fixed set of stationary network assumptions and considers several routing attacks.
S0048.interpretation: It supplies relevant comparisons for online learning and drift-triggered response. Its routing-protocol observations and labels differ substantially from cloud API audit records, so any transfer to CloudTrail is methodological rather than an established performance result.

S0094.summary: E-XAI evaluates SHAP and LIME rather than proposing only another intrusion classifier. It considers descriptive accuracy, sparsity, stability, efficiency, robustness and completeness across multiple intrusion datasets and model families. Both global explanations and local explanations are examined, and code is made available for reuse.
S0094.interpretation: This is an important methodological comparator because explanation quality has several dimensions. A stable ranking can still be unfaithful, while a faithful explanation may be too expensive for frequent monitoring. Classification accuracy alone cannot resolve those trade-offs.

S0095.summary: The authors study the applicability of SHAP and LIME to a multilayer-perceptron intrusion detector. Perturbation-based analysis and a survey are used to examine how explanations help users interpret predictions and compare the two explanation approaches. The focus is on understanding model behaviour rather than introducing a temporal drift alarm.
S0095.interpretation: The work supports evaluating usefulness and model response instead of relying solely on attractive importance plots. Survey findings and perturbation tests should retain their original participants, setting and scope if used for numerical comparisons.

S0115.summary: This Industry 5.0 detector combines bidirectional LSTM and GRU components with fully connected classification layers. SHAP is applied to identify the features contributing to its predictions. The reported experiments use CICDDoS2019 and compare the detector with other approaches to network attack identification.
S0115.interpretation: The model combines sequence learning with post-hoc interpretation. An explanation of a correct prediction does not independently verify cyber resilience, and neither bidirectional sequence modelling nor dataset performance alone establishes a causal streaming evaluation.

S0129.summary: X-CANIDS turns CAN message payloads into human-readable signals using a CAN database. Those signals support intrusion detection and help indicate which signal or electronic control unit may be affected. The study also tests feasibility on automotive-grade embedded hardware with a GPU.
S0129.interpretation: The main lesson is that explanations become more useful when features retain domain meaning. A similar principle favours interpretable API, identity and service fields in CloudTrail, although CAN behaviour and AWS audit events require different models and validation.

S0139.summary: This distributed framework studies deep learning for online intrusion detection across multiple sensors. It addresses changing benign traffic and previously unseen attacks, comparing continual model adaptation with sequential packet labelling. CNN and LSTM configurations have different roles in learning new flow patterns and detecting attacks early in a sequence.
S0139.interpretation: The paper makes update-data requirements and observation length relevant evaluation variables. Those costs should be included when comparing an adaptive detector with a static model, and should not be hidden behind a single aggregate detection rate.

S0385.summary: The proposed detector combines Spark processing, particle-swarm-optimised clustering and explanation techniques. Spark supports larger-scale data processing, while PSO addresses weaknesses of clustering initialisation and convergence. The work evaluates detection and scalability and provides local and broader interpretations of intrusion recommendations.
S0385.interpretation: This contributes an unsupervised and distributed comparison point. Clustering explanations can support an analyst, but they do not establish that anomalous records are attacks or determine whether updating a model with those records is safe.

E310.summary: This study uses SHAP-based interpretation to select features for encrypted-traffic intrusion detection, discussing the selection process through a causality-oriented lens. CNN and Random Forest models are evaluated on CICIDS2017 and NSL-KDD. The objective is to reduce the input set while retaining useful detection performance.
E310.interpretation: The method links explanations to a concrete model-design decision. A causal interpretation of feature importance requires assumptions beyond a SHAP ranking; the review therefore treats the reported procedure as explanation-guided selection unless stronger causal evidence is demonstrated.

S0026.summary: OIFIDS optimises an Isolation Forest for heterogeneous and streaming industrial-IoT data. A modified Harris Hawks optimisation procedure is used to improve feature and model choices. Evaluation on NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15 and CICIDS-2018 includes detection metrics, computational considerations and streaming behaviour.
S0026.interpretation: This is a relevant detector-family comparator for the CloudTrail project. Its optimisation budget and labelled benchmark assumptions need to be matched fairly; improvements on network-flow datasets are not direct evidence of better drift diagnosis on audit logs.

E406.summary: The EED framework combines three one-dimensional LSTM classifiers through a meta-learner, then explains the ensemble using SHAP. The experiments compare attack identification and interpretation with conventional detection methods. Its two-phase structure separates predictive modelling from the explanation of the resulting classifications.
E406.interpretation: The approach illustrates how explanation can be added to an ensemble. Evaluating ensemble accuracy and explaining influential features does not by itself test explanation stability over time or whether those explanations improve update decisions.

S0137.summary: HAEnID combines stacking, Bayesian model averaging and conditional ensemble components for intrusion detection. Its reported evaluation uses CIC-IDS2017 and explores feature-selection configurations. The paper positions explanation and reduction of false alarms alongside predictive performance.
S0137.interpretation: This is useful for comparisons between ensemble designs, but adaptive weighting inside a classifier should not be equated with an independently validated response to temporal concept drift. Comparable preprocessing, partitioning and tuning budgets remain necessary.

E165.summary: XAPT combines PCA reconstruction-based anomaly scores with Bayesian-network inference of attack stages. SHAP explains how the anomaly information and other features influence stage classification. The study focuses on interpretable analysis of advanced persistent threat campaigns rather than only binary attack detection.
E165.interpretation: It shows why the unit of prediction must be explicit: attack-stage classification, event anomaly detection and drift diagnosis are different tasks. A useful future comparison would preserve the same event grouping and label definitions across those tasks.

S0204.summary: AutoSHARC is a feedback-driven intrusion-detection framework that connects explanation-guided feature selection with post-hoc retraining for QoS-sensitive IoT networks. Its use of Boruta and LightGBM-SHAP links feature relevance with the detector's maintenance process, rather than treating explanations only as a final visualisation.
S0204.interpretation: This is close prior work and must be discussed when positioning a SHAP-guided adaptation project. The mere combination of SHAP and retraining is not a defensible novelty claim. Feedback availability, update criteria and the evaluation of retraining outcomes are the important distinctions.

E316.summary: The study evaluates adaptive self-adjusting-memory k-nearest-neighbour learning for IoT and industrial-IoT intrusion detection. It emphasises the ability to retain useful information while managing memory and inference cost in the presence of unfamiliar attacks. Reported comparisons include predictive and resource-efficiency outcomes.
E316.interpretation: A memory-based online learner offers a useful alternative to repeatedly retraining a batch model. A fair comparison must specify how labels arrive and whether each policy sees the same observations and update opportunities.

S0245.summary: XI2S-IDS uses two classification stages to address low-frequency attacks. A binary stage first separates benign and suspicious traffic, followed by more specific attack classification. SHAP explains the decisions, and UNSW-NB15 and CICIDS2017 are used in the evaluation.
S0245.interpretation: The paper highlights why aggregate accuracy may conceal missed rare attacks. For a CloudTrail comparison, per-class recall and the cost of the first-stage routing decision would be more informative than a pooled score across incompatible label sets.

E317.summary: This log-anomaly study introduces Loss with Decaying Factor to reduce the influence of older training information. It combines that objective with a domain-specific pretrained language model and evaluates transfer across heterogeneous log environments. The motivation is that log structures, vocabulary and event frequencies can change between systems.
E317.interpretation: Temporal weighting is directly relevant to maintaining log detectors. Recency, however, is not itself evidence that a new record is benign. Safe adaptation still requires controls against learning attack activity and evaluation on genuinely later, unseen observations.

S0021.summary: The authors represent smart-grid network traces for evaluation with several deep-learning architectures. Grad-CAM++ and Score-CAM highlight the image regions contributing to attack predictions, and an image-similarity measure compares explanation outputs. The paper reports experiments using more than one dataset.
S0021.interpretation: This provides a non-SHAP example of explaining security decisions. Visual saliency over an encoded trace is not directly interchangeable with attribution to meaningful CloudTrail fields, and similarity between saliency maps does not prove causal correctness.

E318.summary: This CAN intrusion-detection study combines LIME with a vision-language model to turn visual explanation outputs into textual descriptions. The authors evaluate their approach on a public CAN intrusion dataset and aim to make model decisions easier for users to interpret.
E318.interpretation: Narratives can make feature evidence more accessible, but fluent text should remain tied to the original attribution and prediction. Any claim that the generated text improves trust or decisions requires an appropriate user evaluation rather than narrative quality alone.

E319.summary: X-FuseRLSTM combines deep and transformer-based feature extraction with attention-guided fusion and residual LSTM classification. Explanations are added to the resulting intrusion predictions, and the authors discuss evaluation across heterogeneous IoT datasets and label configurations.
E319.interpretation: The framework is relevant to the representation choices involved in cross-domain security monitoring. Cross-dataset results should retain their feature harmonisation, label mappings and training conditions; they are not automatically evidence of zero-shot deployment in an unrelated cloud audit domain.

E055.summary: XAI-XGBoost addresses class imbalance and interpretability in medical-IoT intrusion detection. Hybrid sampling, recursive feature elimination and XGBoost classification are combined with SHAP and LIME. WUSTL-EHMS-2020 supplies network-flow and biometric information for the reported evaluation.
E055.interpretation: This is a transparent tabular-detector comparator, especially for inspecting sampling and feature-selection effects. Its clinical-network data and explanations do not independently validate drift monitoring or attack detection in CloudTrail.

E321.summary: The ML-CCPS framework organises medical-IoT security as a feedback loop involving feature modelling, behavioural analysis and extreme-learning-machine classification. The authors evaluate detection and access-control behaviour on CICIoT2023 and discuss noise tolerance, resource constraints and scaling with connected devices.
E321.interpretation: The work broadens adaptation beyond detector refitting to include operational response. Those response claims should be assessed separately from classification performance, with particular attention to how intervention outcomes and novel-attack labels are established.

S0140.summary: This approach pairs a lightweight one-dimensional CNN with SHAP and LIME for IoT intrusion detection. The evaluation uses ToN-IoT and reports predictive outcomes together with interpretation of the model's decisions. Its stated goal is to support resource-constrained devices without losing decision transparency.
S0140.interpretation: The study offers a relatively compact deep-learning comparator. Model size, explanation computation and deployment latency should be measured separately, since a lightweight predictor can still require an expensive explanation stage.

E059.summary: XAICR-HDLOA combines scaling, optimisation-based feature selection and a hybrid CNN-recurrent detector. An improved Chimp Optimizer tunes the model, while SHAP provides feature-level interpretation. The reported experiments use Edge-IIoT and BoT-IoT and compare the resulting detection performance with other methods.
E059.interpretation: The many pipeline components make ablation and tuning-budget fairness particularly important. Better classification after optimisation would not, by itself, show that the explanation stage caused the gain or that the model is robust to future drift.

E053.summary: The study combines dimensionality reduction, an optimised learning pipeline and explainability for intrusion detection. NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017 are used to assess the proposed EIDCDR-XAIADL framework. The motivation is to reduce feature complexity while making automatically generated security decisions understandable.
E053.interpretation: This is relevant to the cost of explaining high-dimensional detectors. When feature transformations are used, a review must identify whether explanations refer to original inputs or transformed dimensions; those interpretations are not equivalent for an analyst.

E066.summary: A self-attention deep neural network uses learnable feature gating to emphasise useful traffic inputs and suppress redundant ones. SHAP and LIME explain the trained classifier. The reported evaluation includes BoT-IoT, N-BaIoT and UNSW-NB15, linking feature optimisation with intrusion classification across several datasets.
E066.interpretation: Learned attention, feature gating and post-hoc attribution represent different forms of information about the model. Agreement among them may be informative, but should not be assumed or treated as evidence of a validated drift diagnosis without a direct test.

E070.summary: FedMedSecure combines federated few-shot learning, cross-attention and a confidence-weighted ensemble for healthcare cybersecurity. The authors also discuss privacy protection and communication compression. The evaluation concerns learning from limited attack examples across distributed participants rather than a single static central classifier.
E070.interpretation: This is useful for separating label efficiency, communication efficiency and interpretability. Claims about privacy require their stated mechanism and threat model; keeping raw records local alone is not proof that updates reveal no information.

E071.summary: The proposed edge-centric intrusion framework coordinates adaptive federated learning under energy and communication constraints. Resource-aware aggregation and model-management components are intended to improve detection while limiting the cost of participation by constrained devices. The authors report comparisons that include operational overhead as well as classification outcomes.
E071.interpretation: Adaptation has a resource budget, not just an accuracy objective. Comparisons with a local CloudTrail prototype must therefore distinguish network and energy costs from model-update decisions and avoid treating them as the same deployment problem.

E074.summary: This study evaluates CNN and ANN attack classifiers on NF-BoT-IoT-V2 and uses SHAP and LIME to explain predictions. It frames the system as a neuro-symbolic architecture and outlines mappings from learned attack patterns to reasoning and consumer-IoT use cases.
E074.interpretation: The evaluated neural classifiers should be distinguished from proposed symbolic integration. A future architectural extension is not the same as an empirically demonstrated reasoning capability, and explanation of a classifier does not establish concept-drift handling.

E079.summary: FL-MalDrift combines local drift detectors with server-side participation control in federated malware learning. ADWIN, DDM, EDDM and HDDM provide local change signals, while smoothed drift scores influence aggregation of client updates. The evaluation includes malware benchmarks and a chronological AndroZoo split.
E079.interpretation: This directly connects monitoring with control of the update stream. It also shows why non-IID client differences and changes over time should be distinguished. Its malware representation is supporting evidence for adaptation policy design, not a ready-made cloud audit benchmark.

E081.summary: The proposed medical-IoT detector combines an initially trained C4.5 decision tree with a Deep Q-Network feedback loop. The tree supplies a low-cost starting decision, while reinforcement learning is intended to improve behaviour as network interactions and attacks vary. The evaluation discusses detection and constrained deployment.
E081.interpretation: A reinforcement-learning update needs a defined reward and observation process. Those supervision and interaction assumptions should be exposed when comparing it with an unsupervised anomaly detector that does not receive an attack label or reward after every event.

S0199.summary: The authors investigate an explainable intrusion pipeline for imbalanced network data. Robust scaling and distribution transformation address skew and outliers, while Harris Hawks optimisation is used within the modelling approach. The paper discusses multi-class intrusion classification and the difficulty of explaining decisions on minority attack classes.
S0199.interpretation: This is relevant to preprocessing and class imbalance, not evidence that an optimiser solves natural temporal drift. Online publication and journal issue years should be kept distinct where the source records differ. Reported metrics require their original dataset and class definitions.

S0202.summary: FedXLog combines distributed log modelling, federated learning and explanation alignment. Hierarchical features address heterogeneous logs, FedGradTrace is used to interpret aggregation trajectories, and knowledge distillation reduces model size. The proposal also uses hash-based feature alignment to support consistency between distributed explanations.
S0202.interpretation: This is a close system-log comparator because it considers explanation meaning across participants. Sharing parameters rather than raw logs reduces centralisation but does not alone prove privacy. Explanation alignment should also be distinguished from detecting a harmful temporal change.

S0203.summary: LEXIS converts classifier predictions and top-ranked attribution evidence into structured incident-report drafts using an LLM. The reporting schema includes suspected causes, confidence cues, false-positive checks and candidate actions for analyst review. The paper explicitly treats the implementation as a benchmark prototype rather than a validated autonomous security operator.
S0203.interpretation: The contribution concerns evidence-bounded communication of explanations. Generated recommendations must remain proposals for review; factual grounding, attribution faithfulness and analyst benefit should be evaluated separately from the detector's classification score.

E398.summary: This healthcare-IoT anomaly detector combines learning, feature selection and explainability within a reinforcement-learning-oriented security framework. The paper evaluates predictive metrics across multiple cyber-threat datasets and discusses threats such as denial of service and scanning in connected healthcare environments.
E398.interpretation: The deployment narrative and the actual evaluated data should remain separate. Benchmark detection performance is relevant supporting evidence, but does not establish clinical effectiveness, safety certification or operation in a live metaverse healthcare service.

S0077.summary: RS2FS selects compact stage-specific feature sets and routes traffic through confidence-gated SVM models and an ANFIS component. The study combines feature screening, relevance analysis and pruning with calibrated classification. Its evaluation includes open-set and perturbation-related checks as well as reported deployment-oriented costs.
S0077.interpretation: Confidence gating and drift handling should be evaluated as distinct mechanisms. Low confidence can trigger additional processing, but high confidence cannot guarantee correctness after a distribution shift; that assumption needs temporal validation.

E082.summary: This HED-ID paper combines a stacked bidirectional GRU, attention and Grey Wolf Optimisation for feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. SHAP relates predictions to network features, while the evaluation discusses detection and resource use in edge-like and cloud-like configurations.
E082.interpretation: Resource measurements make the predictor easier to assess operationally, but should not be extended to an AWS deployment that was not tested. This article is distinct from the later federated HED-ID study and must not be merged merely because the acronym is shared.

E097.summary: HeXAI-AttentionCPS combines an attention-based few-shot LSTM with focal loss and PCA to address imbalanced cyber-physical network data. SHAP supplies feature-contribution explanations, and ToN-IoT2020 is used for evaluation. The authors compare detection quality and false positives with other intrusion methods.
E097.interpretation: Few-shot results depend on how support examples and held-out classes are chosen. PCA also makes it important to identify the level at which attributions are interpreted; transformed components do not automatically correspond to original operational fields.

S0002.summary: The cGGReaT approach uses a pretrained DistilGPT-2-based generator to increase representation of minority classes in tabular security data. The study evaluates classifiers on UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2017, incorporates drift-related maintenance and uses SHAP and LIME to interpret model behaviour.
S0002.interpretation: Synthetic balancing changes the training distribution and therefore needs careful separation from test data. Better classification on a balanced benchmark does not by itself demonstrate safe adaptation to a naturally evolving deployment or reliable explanations on unmodified future traffic.

E088.summary: This smart-grid study combines disturbance and cyberattack detection using synchronised measurements, feature selection and ensemble learning. Explanation is intended to help distinguish physical failures from malicious manipulation, rather than treating those event types as independent detection problems.
E088.interpretation: The distinction between benign operational change and security-relevant change is useful to the CloudTrail research question. Power-system signals and labels are nevertheless domain-specific, so their reported performance is methodological context rather than evidence of cloud-audit transfer.

E336.summary: GCN-DQN combines graph convolution with multi-head attention and a Deep Q-Network that adjusts attention weights. Its intrusion-detection experiments use UNSW-NB15 and CICIDS2017. SHAP and LIME provide additional explanations of the resulting predictions.
E336.interpretation: Adaptive attention inside a trained architecture should not be mistaken for detecting a change in deployment data. The review should distinguish graph construction, classifier optimisation, explanation and temporal model maintenance as separate contributions.

S0142.summary: REACT-D3QN uses a duelling double-Q architecture and an asymmetric reward to prioritise attack recall during cross-dataset transition. The reported protocol moves from CIC-IDS2017 to CIC-IDS2018 with a reduced feature set. The paper presents resilience to changed traffic as an architectural and reward-design objective.
S0142.interpretation: Emphasising recall can change the balance of missed attacks and false alarms. A high recall result must therefore be reported alongside the false-positive rate, reward availability and adaptation conditions, rather than used alone to claim a universally better security policy.

E214.summary: NIDS-beta integrates transformer-style semantic representations with statistical flow features. Attention visualisations and SHAP are used to explain attack decisions, while evaluation on CIC-IDS2018 and UNSW-NB15 includes classification, calibration and unfamiliar-attack settings.
E214.interpretation: Combining semantic and numeric inputs is relevant to log interpretation. The claimed contextual reasoning should be checked against the actual inputs and experiments; architecture terminology alone does not establish reliable reasoning about a real security incident.

E106.summary: This multi-component intrusion framework addresses missing values, out-of-order traffic and uncertainty through imputation, clustering, neutrosophic reasoning and recurrent learning. It also considers alert prioritisation and explanation. The motivation is to reduce errors arising when network observations are incomplete or poorly ordered.
E106.interpretation: Data-quality uncertainty is a useful additional cause of apparent model change. Missing values, delayed packets, natural drift and adversarial behaviour should not be pooled as one phenomenon; controlled ablations are needed to attribute any benefit to a particular component.

S0031.summary: FedTran combines resampling, feature optimisation, transfer learning and federated training for intrusion detection. Tabular features are mapped into image-like representations for pretrained vision models, and SHAP is used for interpretation. The reported evaluation includes UNSW-NB15 and compares central transfer-learning and federated configurations.
S0031.interpretation: Different training configurations must not be treated as a single comparable score. Image encoding also changes feature semantics, making it necessary to check how explanations are translated back to the original security fields.

E109.summary: This Android-malware framework combines CatBoost feature selection, few-shot prototypical learning, a quantum-enhanced component and drift detection. SHAP and LIME are used for interpretation, with CCCS-CIC-AndMal-2020 and KronoDroid among the evaluated data sources. The method aims to learn emerging families from few labelled support examples.
E109.interpretation: The work is relevant to limited-label adaptation but has a different observation space from cloud events. Its few-shot and drift experiments need to be distinguished from a naturally chronological test, and from evidence that the quantum component itself caused a gain.

E110.summary: FeXAI combines federated learning with explanation for cyber-threat detection in smart transportation. The application scope includes vehicular communication and electric-vehicle charging systems. The reported experiments use multiple IoT security datasets and consider distributed learning instead of centrally pooling raw records.
E110.interpretation: This gives supporting evidence for distributed explanation and data heterogeneity. Results across related transportation datasets should not be restated as a test on AWS identities or API logs; the same distinction applies to privacy claims and operational deployment claims.

E184.summary: MedDefender-MHAN combines convolutional features with transformer-based dependency modelling in a multi-head attention architecture. It positions explanations within the model rather than solely as a later post-hoc step. The study evaluates healthcare-IoT threat detection and compares aspects of explanation with methods such as SHAP and Integrated Gradients.
E184.interpretation: Attention-based transparency and post-hoc attribution require independent faithfulness tests. The review does not adopt regulatory-compliance or clinical-readiness claims solely from a benchmark article; those require evidence beyond classification and explanation results.

E119.summary: HDCI-Net integrates convolutional, recurrent, fuzzy and adversarial learning for cross-domain intrusion detection. The paper describes a harmonised multi-domain dataset, UniSec-Fusion2025, assembled from several traffic sources and prototype captures. Feature harmonisation and interpretability are central to the proposed workflow.
E119.interpretation: A merged dataset does not automatically create independent external validation. The review should distinguish training and testing within a harmonised collection from transfer to an untouched environment, and should retain the provenance of each contributing source.

E126.summary: The proposed two-stage intrusion pipeline combines a Feature-Token Transformer and variational autoencoder with class-balanced loss and precision-oriented routing. Probability calibration, temperature scaling and threshold optimisation are part of the stated reliability objective. The study treats confidence quality and false alarms as outcomes in addition to classification.
E126.interpretation: Calibrated risk is relevant to deciding whether to adapt, but calibration must be estimated on held-out data. A threshold tuned on the final target batch should not be presented as evidence of prospective deployment performance.

E344.summary: This evaluation compares SHAP and LIME under DeepFool perturbations using several intrusion datasets and classifier families. Sparsity, completeness and robustness are measured. The authors report trade-offs: stronger feature alignment and completeness do not necessarily coincide with the most stable top-ranked feature set.
E344.interpretation: The study argues against treating one explanation metric as a complete reliability measure. A coupling-based drift diagnosis should therefore be tested for both attribution movement and explanation fidelity, including under perturbations that leave the intended security meaning unchanged.

E116.summary: The authors combine graph-aware learning with adversarial training for IoT intrusion detection. FGSM, DeepFool and combined perturbation settings support robustness evaluation, and a derived adversarial dataset is discussed. The approach also adds explanation to help interpret decisions under manipulated traffic.
E116.interpretation: Feature-space robustness tests are useful but need feasibility checks: a numerical perturbation may not correspond to traffic an attacker can actually generate. Those limits should remain visible when relating adversarial explanation instability to operational security risk.

E128.summary: This cloud-log study compares NLP representations such as TF-IDF, BERT and Word2Vec before classification with a particle-swarm-optimised LightGBM model. SHAP explains how the resulting inputs influence anomaly decisions. The paper evaluates multiple preprocessing configurations rather than relying on a single representation.
E128.interpretation: Representation choice is an important source of model behaviour and explanation changes. Its system-log results should be kept separate from labelled cloud API attack detection, and hyperparameter-search costs should be included in a fair efficiency comparison.

E132.summary: EMT-IDNet combines network traffic, host logs and IoT telemetry through modality-specific encoders and cross-modal attention. A temporal component models attack sequences, while explanation is intended to identify influential modalities and time points. The study reports multimodal intrusion-detection experiments.
E132.interpretation: The work motivates using complementary evidence instead of a single marginal statistic. However, attention to a modality is not proof of a causal attack source, and multimodal gains depend on whether the additional observations would be available at inference time.

E346.summary: AMM-HFL uses client, edge and cloud tiers with similarity-aware clustering and multiple global models. Dynamic client-side model selection addresses heterogeneous data, while clustering of updates is intended to isolate anomalous contributions. The evaluation includes IID and non-IID conditions on IDSIoT2024.
E346.interpretation: The framework is useful for thinking about a single detector's limits across environments. Client heterogeneity, adversarial update filtering and temporal concept drift are related but different challenges, and each requires a distinct evaluation condition.

E199.summary: The proposed deep feature-selection method trains a CNN-BiLSTM and uses permutation importance to rank original intrusion inputs. The authors compare the selected features with alternatives such as mutual information, including in imbalanced settings. Offline selection is separated from the later inference pipeline.
E199.interpretation: Permutation importance supplies an alternative to SHAP for testing whether an explanation-dependent policy is method-specific. Rankings depend on feature correlation and the evaluation distribution, so apparent agreement or disagreement needs to be interpreted with those dependencies in mind.

E131.summary: The proposed cloud-firewall architecture combines LSTM traffic analysis, federated learning, adaptive policy response and audit-related components. It also discusses zero-trust and post-quantum security mechanisms. The paper's broad objective is coordinated protection across cloud-service settings rather than a single isolated anomaly score.
E131.interpretation: Architectural breadth does not establish that each component has been independently validated. Traffic classification, firewall intervention, cryptographic protection and audit integrity should retain separate evidence and costs when the work is compared with a CloudTrail drift prototype.

E134.summary: This parser-free log-anomaly model fine-tunes a BERT-based architecture and uses SHAP to explain individual log entries. Subword attributions are mapped to word-level importance so an operator can read the explanation in the original message. The study reports within-domain and cross-domain detection settings and processing throughput.
E134.interpretation: Its treatment of explanation granularity is directly useful for log monitoring. Attribution changes can result from tokenisation or vocabulary shifts, so an explanation-drift alarm should distinguish those representation changes from evidence that security decisions have become less reliable.

E137.summary: The authors combine a CNN-Transformer classifier, FedAvg aggregation and LIME explanations for distributed IoT intrusion detection. The model learns local patterns and longer-range dependencies while keeping data at participating sites. The reported evaluation includes multi-class classification and additional dataset-based checks.
E137.interpretation: The pipeline offers a useful comparison for distributed model explanation. Keeping data local and producing an explanation are separate properties; neither establishes robustness to malicious updates, privacy guarantees or future drift without its own supporting test.

E033.summary: This forensic-oriented method documents a Random Forest intrusion workflow on ToN-IoT, including partitioning, deterministic preprocessing, SHAP and LIME, interaction-graph construction and counterfactual analysis. It also releases intermediate artifacts intended to make the analysis reproducible and auditable.
E033.interpretation: The work is especially relevant to evidence traceability. A counterfactual change that alters a prediction is not automatically a feasible attacker action or remediation, and a reproducible static pipeline still needs separate evaluation before serving as a drift-monitoring policy.

E218.summary: The proposed M3-GAZE framework combines evolution-aware learning, adversarial augmentation and uncertainty analysis for zero-day threat detection. A graph-based component represents the proposed evolution and propagation of threats, and the paper reports improvements in rare-threat detection and adaptation under its evaluated settings.
E218.interpretation: The reviewer should distinguish a designed causal or evolutionary representation from empirically established causal relationships. Support-set construction, synthetic augmentation and uncertainty calibration are important assumptions when interpreting claims about genuinely unseen attacks.

E219.summary: This study compares attention-enhanced CNN, LSTM and GRU intrusion models and applies SHAP to their multi-class predictions. The approach is evaluated on IoT security data and aims to identify which traffic features influence different attack classifications. Both spatial feature extraction and temporal representation are considered.
E219.interpretation: Attention and SHAP can provide complementary information, but their agreement should be measured rather than assumed. A change in important features across attack classes is also different from an unexplained change over deployment time.

E140.summary: RADIUS uses a temporal convolutional encoder and an adaptive state-transition module for software-defined IoT intrusion detection. Its training objective incorporates invariance and state-related structure, with evaluation of detection and model components. The intention is to handle heterogeneous and changing traffic more reliably.
E140.interpretation: Invariant representation learning is a useful alternative to frequent retraining. Whether it actually limits temporal degradation must be tested on ordered observations, rather than inferred from a static accuracy comparison or the presence of an adaptive module.

S0034.summary: ADAWU-IDS combines a multi-scale drift-severity index with adaptive ensemble weighting and validation-calibrated response control. Candidate response settings are selected on validation data before final chronological evaluation. The paper explicitly avoids assuming that stronger adaptation must always improve detection and reports component-level and statistical analyses.
S0034.interpretation: This is particularly close prior work for risk-sensitive adaptation. A new contribution should be justified through matched prospective comparisons and identifiable additional evidence, not through the general idea of combining a drift signal with an adaptive response.

E223.summary: GeoGuard-PTI combines spatiotemporal threat forecasting with a closed-loop defensive response. Its evaluation draws on intrusion benchmarks augmented with synthetic geographic propagation traces. Graph attention and temporal diffusion components are used to generate forecasts at several horizons and inform intervention.
E223.interpretation: The geographic and propagation information is partly constructed, which limits what the experiment establishes about real attack forecasting. Forecast accuracy and intervention outcomes must retain their synthetic-data context rather than being treated as independent field evidence.

S0017.summary: This distributed log detector combines a modified Drain parser with improved HDBSCAN clustering on Spark. Spatial indexing and minimum-spanning-tree optimisation address computational costs, while cross-partition fusion supports anomaly scoring. The reported datasets include HDFS, BGL and OpenStack.
S0017.interpretation: It supplies an unsupervised, scalable log-analysis baseline. An operational anomaly in these datasets is not necessarily an attack, and improvements in parsing efficiency should be kept separate from evidence of security detection or safe model adaptation.

E008.summary: Logs2Graphs converts event logs into directed, weighted graphs and applies a one-class graph neural network, OCDiGCN, to detect anomalous graph instances. Selected graph nodes provide explanations of a detected anomaly. The reported experiments use five benchmark datasets and compare against other log-anomaly approaches.
E008.interpretation: This demonstrates a relational alternative to tabular feature attributions. Graph-level explanations and event-level SHAP values have different units, so comparisons should align the anomaly target and explanation granularity before making claims about superiority.

E356.summary: AHGA-SA combines a genetic algorithm with simulated annealing to select compact feature subsets for IoT intrusion detection. SHAP explains the contribution of retained features. The study reports experiments on recent intrusion benchmarks and considers training cost, testing cost, memory and feature count as well as detection performance.
E356.interpretation: The paper makes feature-selection overhead visible, which is useful for cost-aware comparisons. An adaptive search algorithm is not automatically an online drift detector, and the effect of the search should be separated from the explanation stage.

E357.summary: The authors partition IoMT network features into semantic groups and train specialised experts. A gated mixture-of-experts mechanism and cross-expert attention combine the representations, while multi-level interpretation examines feature contributions and expert specialisation. The evaluation concerns multi-class medical-IoT intrusion detection.
E357.interpretation: Semantic feature groups may make explanations more operationally meaningful. Routing changes between experts are nevertheless not a direct measure of concept drift, and attention-based interpretation still requires a faithfulness check.

E148.summary: This SDN intrusion pipeline uses GAN-based balancing, ANOVA and genetic feature selection, classifier optimisation and explainability. It targets imbalanced multi-class network data and reports comparisons among tuned classifiers. The design links feature reduction with the interpretation of selected traffic attributes.
E148.interpretation: Resampling, feature selection and tuning can each affect reported gains. Their operations must remain confined to the training process, and a comparison of explanation-guided adaptation should not inherit a static benchmark's score as its own expected outcome.

E360.summary: HDATL-XAI combines Random Forest and SelectKBest feature selection with deep-autoencoder anomaly modelling and classification. Explanation methods are added to make the resulting security decisions more transparent. The paper discusses detection of unfamiliar patterns under controlled experimental conditions.
E360.interpretation: The distinction between controlled unfamiliar patterns and future real-world attacks is important. An autoencoder's deviation score identifies departure from learned behaviour, not necessarily malicious intent, and should be assessed alongside false alarms on benign changes.

E156.summary: This cyber-deception framework uses behavioural features and a Random Forest to classify sessions, then combines explanation, profiling and adaptive environment mutation. Its goal is to make honeypots respond more intelligently to attacker interaction while retaining an interpretable decision process.
E156.interpretation: The study connects detection with an active response, but that changes the observed environment. Evaluation should distinguish improved classification from altered attacker behaviour and should make the control policy and feedback source explicit.

E366.summary: The proposed IoT framework combines supervised Random Forest classification, unsupervised Isolation Forest monitoring and Kolmogorov-Smirnov change analysis. It evaluates detection and includes a held-out attack-family experiment. The authors explicitly limit the interpretation of that experiment rather than claiming comprehensive zero-day coverage.
E366.interpretation: This is a close comparator for combining complementary monitoring signals. Its held-out-family evidence supports a specific controlled claim; it does not establish that every future attack is detectable or that a distribution shift always calls for retraining.

S0081.summary: AgroCyberShield uses a CNN-BiLSTM-attention detector for smart-farming network security. SHAP provides explanation, while the paper reports dataset comparisons, ablations and edge-oriented measurements. The motivation combines evolving traffic, limited device resources and the need for interpretable decisions.
S0081.interpretation: Its agricultural application is supporting cross-domain evidence. The review should separate measured edge performance from claims about generalisation, and should not present two benchmark sources as proof that the method transfers to cloud identity and API activity.

E231.summary: TAE-IDS combines heterogeneous base classifiers with uncertainty-related meta-features and attention-based ensemble learning. SHAP explains the decisions, and a blockchain-inspired mechanism records intrusion information in a tamper-evident form. The study presents classification and traceability as complementary properties.
E231.interpretation: Integrity of a stored alert does not establish that the alert is correct. Predictive accuracy, calibration, explanation faithfulness and record integrity should therefore remain separate evaluation dimensions rather than a single claim of trustworthiness.

E373.summary: This federated SDN intrusion framework combines distributed key generation, threshold homomorphic encryption and collaborative decryption with SHAP explanations. The objective is to avoid a single cryptographic authority while preserving collaborative model learning. Its evaluation discusses detection and the computational costs of the protection mechanisms.
E373.interpretation: The cryptographic threat model and explanation mechanism are distinct contributions. Any claim about deployment feasibility must include encryption, communication and explanation overhead, not only the classifier's inference time.

E159.summary: FedShield-IDS combines a federated one-dimensional CNN-LSTM with SHAP-gated explanations for smart-home intrusion detection. The paper evaluates detection on CICIoT2023 and reports additional cross-dataset testing on Edge-IIoTset, alongside a threshold-sensitivity analysis of the mitigation mechanism.
E159.interpretation: This is relevant to explanation-assisted response and transfer testing. The exact role of target data and threshold calibration remains essential: a separate dataset does not imply label-free prospective transfer unless its use during development is clearly restricted.

E202.summary: IOTTRUST enriches UNSW-NB15 flow classification with graph-topology features. The study explicitly computes topology from the training partition before propagating features to the test partition and compares several modelling tracks. It also inspects which graph features remain influential under the stricter protocol.
E202.interpretation: The paper is useful for explaining how leakage controls can alter apparently strong results. An informative graph feature can still be dataset-specific, so performance on one network topology should not be presumed to generalise to new identities, hosts or clouds.

S0005.summary: This study examines adversarial transfer between XGBoost and LightGBM intrusion models on CICIDS2017 and NSL-KDD. Feature-importance similarity is used to form a heuristic assessment of cross-model vulnerability, alongside direct perturbation tests. The authors describe the relationship as an approximation rather than a deterministic predictor.
S0005.interpretation: It provides a close comparison for reasoning from attribution similarity. Correlated importance vectors can support a hypothesis about shared sensitivity, but direct evaluation is still needed before interpreting a coupling score as a reliable measure of security risk.

E152.summary: The later federated HED-ID study combines a BiGRU-attention detector with resource-adaptive optimisation and aggregated local SHAP explanations. It also discusses retraining interventions in a simulated edge-device setting. This is a separate article from the earlier non-federated HED-ID design.
E152.interpretation: The shared acronym must not cause the two studies or their results to be merged. Simulated annual retraining counts describe that experiment's model of deployment, not observed long-term field operation or a demonstrated CloudTrail maintenance schedule.

E155.summary: X-THREAT combines VAE-GAN augmentation, CNN-BiLSTM-attention detection and context-aware SHAP for rare and unfamiliar attacks. The study evaluates CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15 and ToN-IoT. It also notes that deployment latency, resource usage and edge feasibility were not explicitly benchmarked.
E155.interpretation: The stated deployment limitation should remain in the synthesis rather than being replaced by an assumption of real-time readiness. Minority-class improvement and zero-day evaluation also require their own class, support-set and partition definitions.

S0082.summary: DriftDroid is a temporal evaluation protocol for Android-malware behaviour rather than a new detector architecture. Historical KronoDroid representations are tested on later AndroZoo samples without target refitting, and controlled adaptation is examined separately. The results highlight degradation associated with changed benign behaviour and sensitivity to representation and adaptation choices.
S0082.interpretation: This is a useful example of separating strong source validation from weaker future-domain performance. Its non-monotonic adaptation findings argue for reporting negative or unstable outcomes rather than assuming that more update data always improves a detector.

E232.summary: This empirical audit examines label-free monitoring and test-time adaptation under a temporal transition between CIC-IDS2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018. Confidence estimates, cross-model agreement and conformal abstention are assessed alongside adaptation and label-shift correction. The central question is whether apparently reassuring monitoring signals track actual detection performance after a security-relevant shift.
E232.interpretation: It is particularly important counterevidence to treating confident or mutually agreeing models as proof of safety. A CloudTrail monitoring study should distinguish observed proxy movement from verified attack-detection performance, especially when target labels are unavailable.

S0220.summary: CyberShield Analytics uses SHAP-guided two-level stacking for binary intrusion detection on UNSW-NB15. It discusses leakage control, calibration, statistical testing and explanation as part of the evaluation. The paper distinguishes the binary prediction task from the dataset's underlying attack categories.
S0220.interpretation: The relevant lesson is to define the task before comparing scores. Binary attack-versus-normal performance cannot be directly compared with multi-class detection, and gains in calibration or statistical reliability should not be restated as a large increase in accuracy.

S0007.summary: ASRAE combines an attention-enhanced residual autoencoder with online drift detection, adaptive thresholds, benign-only adversarial training, Integrated Gradients and a later few-shot adaptation stage. The evaluation includes intrusion benchmarks, controlled simulated drift, adversarial perturbations and held-out attack families.
S0007.interpretation: The separate branches of the experiment must retain their supervision assumptions. Benign-only training does not make a later labelled few-shot adaptation phase unsupervised, and simulated drift results do not establish sustained field performance.

S0006.summary: TRINITY-IDS combines statistical, temporal and graph-based views of intrusion traffic with adaptive fusion and evidential uncertainty. Page-Hinkley monitoring and experience replay support continual adaptation, while resampling and feature-selection components address imbalance and dataset dependence.
S0006.interpretation: The rich architecture requires careful ablation before attributing improvement to drift monitoring or uncertainty. Its empirical claims should also be reconciled with any inconsistent data-availability statement, rather than assuming that an open-access article necessarily provides reproducible data and code.
